name: Puerto Rico
context:
Puerto Rico shows zero tracked bills here, and that number is wrong about the territory. It is a tracking gap, not a record of legislative inactivity. LegiScan coverage of the Puerto Rico Legislative Assembly is thin compared with its coverage of the fifty states, and the Assembly conducts its business in Spanish, so keyword matching tuned to English AI vocabulary misses most of what happens. During 2025 and 2026 roughly fourteen artificial intelligence measures moved through the Assembly. Five became law in 2026, three were vetoed, and the rest remain in process. That is a heavier AI legislative output than many states with far higher tracked counts.

The enacted laws cluster around transparency and personal protection rather than industry regulation. Law 105 of 2026, from Senate Project 101 and signed on 10 June 2026, requires that any political advertisement created or modified in whole or in part using artificial intelligence carry a clear disclosure of its origin, amending the electoral code and campaign finance law to cover traditional and digital media. Law 116 of 2026, from Senate Project 622, requires transparency about artificial intelligence in government services so that a resident knows when an interaction is automated. Law 163 of 2026, from Senate Project 441, protects a person's image against unauthorized AI cloning. Law 140 of 2026, from House Project 824 and signed on 23 July 2026, folds artificial intelligence topics into the continuing education and virtual training programs required under the territory's cybersecurity law, covering privacy, system security, data handling, attack prevention and responsible use of new technologies for government information officers and public servants. A joint resolution directs agencies to teach artificial intelligence in vocational schools.

The vetoes are as informative as the signatures. Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez vetoed House Project 347, which would have made the Puerto Rico Innovation and Technology Service the territory's AI regulator with penalty authority, along with Senate Project 705 on AI in sports training and Senate Project 769, which would have created an Artificial Intelligence Development and Innovation Institute funded at ten million dollars a year. The stated ground for the Senate Project 769 veto, issued on 3 June 2026, was that the measure created new fiscal obligations and tax benefits incompatible with the current fiscal plan and with fiscal neutrality. Puerto Rico's fiscal oversight constraints, not policy disagreement about artificial intelligence, are what killed the territory's most ambitious AI institution building. Measures still pending include Senate Project 68, a general government AI regulatory framework, and Senate Project 731, which would centralize public procurement on an AI enhanced platform.

Existing law reaches AI conduct in Puerto Rico through several older statutes. Law 111 of 2005, the Ley de Informacion al Ciudadano sobre la Seguridad de Bancos de Informacion, requires entities holding databases of residents' personal information to notify people of security breaches promptly and in clear and conspicuous form, with fines from 500 to 5,000 dollars per violation, enforced by the Department of Consumer Affairs for private entities and by the Ombudsman for government agencies. Law 39 of 2012 requires online operators to publish and honor accurate privacy policies. Law 38 of 2016 limits commercial collection of consumers' personal information at the point of transaction. The Department of Consumer Affairs, known as DACO, holds general authority over deceptive and unfair commercial practices.

On enforcement, the Department of Justice has invested in internal capacity, running annual conference training for prosecutors, government attorneys and property registrars on the legal impact of artificial intelligence. No external artificial intelligence investigation or enforcement action against a company has been identified.

reading.body:
Puerto Rico has no AI-specific legislation tracked in this database as of September 2026.

This absence is notable because it contrasts with mainland US states and territories that have begun regulating AI systems. Puerto Rico's regulatory silence leaves the jurisdiction without formal legal frameworks governing AI development, deployment, or liability, even as computational activity increasingly drives economic decisions.

The lack of AI law does not indicate that AI systems are unused in Puerto Rico. It suggests instead that AI governance, if it occurs, relies on federal frameworks, corporate policies, or imported standards rather than local legislation. For jurisdictions competing on infrastructure investment, the absence of specific AI rules can be either an advantage (regulatory clarity through openness) or a liability (regulatory uncertainty that deters investment).

This data does not capture executive orders, agency guidance, industry standards, or enforcement actions. It reflects only formal bills in the legislative record.
